name: Advanced Python
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Decorators, context managers, itertools, functools, typing in depth, error patterns, profiling and asyncio.

lesson.intro: This pack covers the Python that shows up in frameworks, libraries and interviews: decorators and closures, context managers, generator pipelines, itertools and functools, advanced typing, enums and pattern matching, error-handling patterns, profiling, and asyncio for real services.
objectives: Write decorators, including ones that take arguments, and your own context managers
Build lazy generator pipelines and use itertools and functools instead of hand-written loops
Read advanced type hints: narrowing, generics, Protocols, TypedDict and Literal
Translate errors at boundaries with from, and handle them at the right layer
Profile before optimizing, and run async work safely with TaskGroup, timeouts and limits

sections.title: Closures and decorators
sections.key: A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper: `@timed` above `def report()` means `report = timed(report)`, which runs once, when the def runs.
sections.body:
Flask routes (`@app.route("/users")`), pytest's `@pytest.mark.parametrize` and `@functools.cache` are all **decorators**, and "write a decorator" is a standard Python interview question.

They rest on **closures**: an inner function keeps the outer function's variables alive after the outer one returns. Each outer call makes a fresh closure with its own state; declare a variable `nonlocal` to rebind it.

Closures capture variables, not values, so every function in `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` returns 2, the final i.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Stacked decorators apply bottom up: `@a` above `@b` above `def f` gives `f = a(b(f))`, so a's wrapper runs first on each call.

steps.label: The def statement creates the original report function
`timed(report)` runs once and returns a wrapper
The name `report` is bound to the wrapper
Each call to `report()` runs the wrapper
The wrapper calls the original and returns its result

visual.title: The shape of a decorator
rows: Accepts any arguments and passes them on
Copies `__name__` and `__doc__`, so logs and tracebacks show the real name
A **decorator factory**: called first, it returns the real decorator

sections.deeper: Where decorators show up in real code: logging and timing, retries, caching (`@functools.cache`), access checks such as `@login_required`, and registration. A registering decorator records the function in a table and returns it unchanged, which is how web frameworks map URLs to your functions: `@app.route("/users")` is a factory call that returns a decorator, and that decorator stores your function under the path.
sections.tip: Always put `@functools.wraps(func)` on the wrapper. Without it every decorated function reports its name as wrapper, which confuses logs, tracebacks and tools.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting `return` in the wrapper. Calling `func(*args, **kwargs)` without returning its value silently turns every decorated function's result into None.

check.question: With @a written above @b above def f, what is the name f bound to?
choices: a(f) and b(f), stored in a tuple
b(a(f))
a(b(f))

check.explanation: Decorators apply from the bottom up: b wraps f first, then a wraps the result. On each call a's wrapper runs first, then b's, then the original f.

sections.title: Writing your own context managers
sections.key: `with` calls `__enter__` (its return value is what `as` binds) and always calls `__exit__`; with `@contextmanager`, put the cleanup in a `finally` around the `yield`.
sections.body:
`with open(...)` closes a file, `with lock:` releases a lock, and `with conn:` commits a transaction or rolls it back. Write your own for any setup whose cleanup must happen: timing a block, a temporary setting, a temp directory.

[[visual]]

For most cases `contextlib.contextmanager` is shorter: a generator that does the setup, `yield`s once (the yielded value is what `as` binds), then cleans up. If the block raises, the exception reappears at the `yield`, so the cleanup must sit in a `finally`.

[[visual 2]]

One `with` can hold several managers, which exit in reverse order. Async code has `async with`, using `__aenter__` and `__aexit__`.

messages.label: __exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)
messages.detail: always; all None if no error

messages.note: Returning True suppresses the exception: code after the block runs

visual.title: contextlib helpers
rows: Ignore one specific exception type, visibly
Enter a variable number of managers; exits them all in reverse
A do-nothing stand-in when a `with` is optional

sections.pitfall: Writing a @contextmanager generator without try/finally around the yield. If the with block raises, the exception appears at the yield and the cleanup after it never runs.

check.question: Your class's __exit__ ends with return True. What happens when the with block raises ValueError?
choices: The ValueError is suppressed and execution continues after the with block
The ValueError propagates to the caller as usual
Python raises TypeError because __exit__ must return None
The block runs a second time
check.explanation: A true return value from __exit__ tells Python the exception has been handled, so it is swallowed. That is useful for suppress(), and a nasty bug anywhere else, which is why most managers return False or None.

sections.title: Generators in depth: yield from, pipelines, re-iteration
sections.key: `yield from` delegates to another iterable, chained generators form lazy pipelines that read nothing until pulled, and a generator can be consumed only once.
sections.body:
Intermediate Python showed that `yield` pauses a function and that generators are lazy and one-shot. Three more ideas make them an everyday tool.

`yield from sub` yields every item of sub, like a for loop around a yield. It shines in recursive generators that walk nested data or a folder tree.

**Pipelines** chain small generators: read, parse, filter, aggregate. Building one runs nothing; the consumer at the end (a for loop, `next()`, `sum()`) pulls one item at a time, so a 20 GB log streams in constant memory.

[[visual]]

**Re-iteration.** A function that loops over its input twice (once for `max`, once to normalize) gets nothing the second time from a generator. A collection class whose `__iter__` is a generator method hands each loop a fresh generator.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: A lazy pipeline
visual.caption: Building the chain reads nothing. Each `next()` makes every stage pull one item from the stage before it.

visual.title: Worth recognizing
rows: Raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield, so a `finally` inside still runs (also when a half-used generator is garbage-collected)
Resumes and makes the paused `yield` evaluate to value; it powered coroutines before async
`(x for x in range(5) if x < limit)`
The first `for` source is evaluated now, but the condition and `limit` only when items are pulled

sections.pitfall: Passing a generator to code that iterates twice. The second pass silently sees nothing; pass a list, or an object whose __iter__ returns a fresh generator.

sections.title: itertools: the iterator toolbox
sections.key: `itertools` turns common loops into lazy one-liners; `groupby` groups only consecutive equal keys, so sort by the same key first.
sections.body:
Data scripts and interview solutions keep needing the same loops: take the first n items, chunk a list, compare neighbors, group records, try every combination. `itertools` has each one as a fast, lazy building block.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

They all return iterators: wrap one in `list()` to look at it, and do not loop twice. Counts explode quickly: all permutations of 10 items is 3,628,800 tuples, fine to stream lazily and slow to build as a list.

visual.title: Streams, combining, aggregating
rows: Endless or repeated streams; stop them with `islice` or `zip`
Slices any iterator, even a file or an infinite generator
Walks several iterables as one; `chain.from_iterable(lists)` flattens one level
Like zip, but pads the shorter input instead of stopping
Chunks of n items; the last may be shorter (3.12+)
Running totals; `accumulate(xs, max)` gives a running max
Groups **consecutive** items with equal keys; it does not sort

sections.code:
from itertools import accumulate, batched, groupby, pairwise

print(list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1])))  # [3, 4, 8, 9]
print(list(pairwise([1, 4, 9])))  # [(1, 4), (4, 9)]
print(list(batched(range(7), 3)))
# [(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6,)]

sales = [("north", 10), ("south", 4), ("north", 7)]
sales.sort(key=lambda s: s[0])  # groupby needs this
for region, rows in groupby(sales, key=lambda s: s[0]):
    print(region, sum(amount for _, amount in rows))
# north 17 / south 4
sections.pitfall: Calling groupby on unsorted data. It only groups neighbors, so north, south, north produces three groups; sort by the same key first.

sections.title: functools: caching, partial and friends
sections.key: `@cache` and `@lru_cache` memoize pure functions with hashable arguments; `partial` pre-fills arguments, and `reduce` folds a sequence into one value.
sections.body:
A few lines of functools can replace a page of code. Its tools take or return functions.

**Caching.** `@cache` and `@lru_cache(maxsize=n)` **memoize** a function: the first call with given arguments runs the body, and later equal calls return the stored result. That turns naive recursion into dynamic programming in one line. `lru_cache` evicts the least recently used entry when full; `cache` never evicts.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Cache rules
rows: Arguments must be hashable: pass a tuple, not a list
They become dict keys, so a list raises TypeError: unhashable type
A result that depends on the time, a database or a live API goes stale forever
The cache keeps every `self` alive, which can leak memory
Report hits and misses; empty the cache

visual.title: More of functools
rows: A new callable with arguments pre-filled, often clearer than a lambda
Folds items into one value by calling `fn(acc, item)`. Without initial, an empty input raises TypeError. Try `sum`, `max` or `math.prod` first
Computed on first access, then stored on the instance
Picks an implementation by the first argument's type
Decorator metadata; fills in `<=`, `>`, `>=` from `__eq__` and `__lt__`

sections.pitfall: Putting @cache on a function whose result depends on the time, a database or a mutable argument. It returns stale answers forever. Cache only pure functions, and bound the size with lru_cache.

activity.title: Memoize a slow recursion
activity.prompt: Run it and note the number of calls. Then import cache from functools and put @cache above def paths. The answer stays the same, and calls drops to the number of distinct (r, c) pairs.

check.question: Why does total([1, 2, 3]) raise TypeError when total is decorated with @cache?
choices: cache requires a maxsize argument
cached functions cannot return integers
cache only works on recursive functions
Lists are unhashable, so they cannot be cache keys; pass a tuple
check.explanation: The cache stores results in a dict keyed by the arguments, so every argument must be hashable. A tuple of the same numbers works.

sections.title: Typing in depth: narrowing, generics, Protocols
sections.key: Check `X | None` before use so the checker narrows it, link input and output types with a type variable, and use Protocols to accept anything with the right methods.
sections.body:
Basic hints such as `int`, `list[str]` and `str | None` cover most signatures. Real codebases use a few more, and you need to read them comfortably.

**Narrowing.** A value typed `X | None` must be checked before you use it as an X. After `if user is None: return`, or inside `if n is not None:`, the checker narrows the type to X; `isinstance` checks narrow too. Most mypy errors in new code are a missing None check.

[[visual]]

None of this changes what happens at runtime. The payoff comes from running mypy or Pyright in your editor and in CI.

visual.title: Reading advanced hints
rows: A **generic** function: T links input and output, so `first([3, 1])` returns `int | None`. Older code declares `T = TypeVar("T")`
A **Protocol**: any object with a matching `close()` fits, with no inheritance needed
A **TypedDict**: a dict with specific keys and value types
A function that takes an int and a str and returns a bool
Switches checking off: a function returning Any disables checks on how every caller uses the result
Accepts anything but allows almost nothing until you narrow it: prefer it to Any
A constant that must not be reassigned; a class-level attribute
Tells the checker to trust you; does nothing at runtime

sections.pitfall: Silencing errors with Any. A function that returns Any quietly turns off checking for every caller; type it properly, use object, or narrow with isinstance.

check.question: def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T | None. What type does a checker infer for first(["a", "b"])?
choices: list[str]
Any
str | None
T
check.explanation: T is bound to str by the argument list[str], so the return type T | None becomes str | None. The None part stays because an empty list returns None.

sections.title: Dataclasses, enums and pattern matching
sections.key: Dataclass options validate and lock down records, Enums replace magic strings, and `match` compares a value against shapes, binding the parts it captures.
sections.body:
Dataclasses are the default way to model records in modern Python. Enums and `match` keep the code that uses those records clean.

[[visual]]

An **Enum** is a fixed set of named constants: `Status.DONE` instead of the string "done", where a typo like "dnoe" is a silent bug. Members have `.name` and `.value`, `Status("done")` looks one up by value (ValueError for anything else), and you can loop over the class. `StrEnum` members are also real strings.

**Structural pattern matching** (`match`, 3.10+) compares a value against shapes:

[[visual 2]]

For a plain lookup of one value, a dict or if/elif is still simpler.

visual.title: Dataclass extras
rows: Runs after the generated `__init__`: validate there and raise ValueError
Every field is keyword-only, so two fields of the same type cannot be swapped
Less memory, and a typo such as `t.titel = "x"` raises AttributeError
Returns a modified copy; the original is unchanged
Converts recursively to dicts and lists (enums and dates still need converting for JSON)

visual.title: Case patterns
rows: A two-item sequence starting with "add"; binds title
Dicts with those keys; extra keys are allowed, and `**rest` captures them
Alternatives, binding a sub-pattern, and a guard
A constant needs a dotted name or a literal
A bare name captures anything; `_` is the catch-all

sections.code:
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    TODO = "todo"
    DONE = "done"

print(Status("done") is Status.DONE)  # True

def handle(command: str) -> str:
    match command.split():
        case ["add", title]:
            return f"adding {title}"
        case ["move", title, ("todo" | "done") as s]:
            return f"moving {title} to {s}"
        case _:
            return "unknown command"

print(handle("move docs done"))  # moving docs to done
sections.pitfall: Writing `case DONE:` with a plain name to compare against a constant. A bare name is a capture pattern that matches anything; use a dotted name such as `case Status.DONE:` or a literal.

    {"type": "key", "key": "Enter"},
    {"type": "key", "key": "q", "ctrl": True},

check.question: What does dataclasses.replace(task, status=Status.DONE) do?
choices: Returns a dict with the new status
Returns a new Task with status changed, leaving task unchanged
Changes task in place and returns it

sections.title: Error-handling patterns for real code
sections.key: Define a small exception hierarchy, translate low-level errors at module boundaries with `raise ... from err`, and handle each error once, at the layer that can act on it.
sections.body:
**A small hierarchy.** One base class (`AppError`) with specific subclasses (`ConfigError`, `NotFound`) lets callers catch one failure, or everything from your code, without catching unrelated bugs.

**Translate at boundaries.** A KeyError means little to whoever called `load_config()`. Catch it at the edge and raise a meaningful error from the original:

[[visual]]

`err.add_note("while processing row 3")` (3.11+) adds context before a bare `raise`. An **ExceptionGroup** carries several independent errors, handled with `except*`.

**Where to handle.** At the layer that can act (retry, show a message, return a 400), usually a request handler or `main()`, logging with `logger.exception(...)`. Logging at every level writes one error five times.

**Retry** only transient failures that are safe to repeat, with capped attempts and exponential backoff:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Raising inside an except block
rows: Shows both, joined by "The above exception was the direct cause...". `err` is kept as `__cause__`
Hides the original: use it when the original is pure noise
"During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred": usually a bug in the handler

items.title: Retry
points: Payments only with an idempotency key

items.title: Do not retry
points: ValueError and other bad input: it fails the same way every time
A charge with no idempotency key: it could happen twice

sections.pitfall: Writing `raise NewError(...)` inside an except block without `from err`. The traceback then reads like a crash in your handler instead of a deliberate translation.

check.question: What does raise ConfigError("bad config") from err add, compared with a plain raise ConfigError("bad config") in the same except block?
choices: It records err as the explicit __cause__, so the traceback shows it as the direct cause
It turns err into a warning
It suppresses err completely
It re-raises err unchanged
check.explanation: from err sets __cause__ and marks the chain as deliberate. Without it, Python still attaches err as __context__, but the traceback reads as if a second error happened while handling the first.

sections.title: Performance: measure, profile, then optimize
sections.key: Measure and profile before optimizing: the fix is usually an algorithm or data structure change, and it only counts if the numbers show it.
sections.body:
Your script takes 40 seconds, so you rewrite the regex you suspect. It still takes 40 seconds: the time went into a list searched inside a loop. Programmers guess badly where time goes, so measure first.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A profile usually reveals an algorithm problem, and Big-O wins dwarf micro-tweaks:

[[visual 3]]

Then come smaller wins: built-ins and comprehensions run in C, `slots=True` cuts memory for millions of objects, NumPy moves numeric loops into C, and multiprocessing spreads CPU-bound work across cores.

steps.label: Measure the slow case with realistic input
Profile to find the biggest cumulative cost
Fix the algorithm or data structure there
Re-measure
steps.detail: Keep the change only if the numbers improve; otherwise revert to the simpler code

visual.title: Measuring tools
rows: A quick number around a block
Runs a snippet many times: `python -m timeit "sorted(range(1000))"`
`python -m cProfile -s cumulative app.py` lists every function with its call count, **tottime** (its own time) and **cumtime** (including everything it called)
Draw a profile; sample a running process without restarting it
Which lines allocate the most memory
visual.caption: Sort by cumtime to find the expensive branch, then by tottime to find the hot function itself.

visual.title: Common fixes
rows: `x in some_list` inside a loop: O(n) each time
Build a set or dict once: O(1)
`s += piece` in a loop: may copy the string each time
Collect pieces in a list, then `"".join(pieces)`
The same work repeated inside a loop
Hoist it out, or cache it
One query for all of them

sections.code:
import timeit

items = list(range(10_000))
as_set = set(items)
t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: 9_999 in items, number=1_000)
t_set = timeit.timeit(lambda: 9_999 in as_set, number=1_000)
print(f"list: {t_list:.4f} s  set: {t_set:.4f} s")
# e.g. list: 0.0409 s  set: 0.0000 s
sections.pitfall: Optimizing before profiling. Rewriting the part you suspect wastes time and adds complexity; profile with realistic data and fix the biggest cumulative cost first.

activity.prompt: Run it and note both times. Then double n to 20_000 and run again: the list version should take roughly four times as long (O(n) work per pop, O(n^2) in total), while the deque version roughly doubles.

check.question: In cProfile output, what does cumtime include that tottime does not?
choices: Time spent compiling the module
Time spent waiting for input
Time spent inside the functions it called
Time spent by other processes
check.explanation: tottime is time spent in the function's own code; cumtime adds everything it called. A main() with a huge cumtime and tiny tottime is just the caller of the slow part.

sections.title: asyncio in depth: TaskGroup, timeouts, queues
sections.key: Run related tasks in a `TaskGroup` so one failure cancels the rest, time out network calls, bound concurrency with a Semaphore or Queue, and never swallow CancelledError.
sections.body:
Real async services (FastAPI apps, scrapers, bots) need more than `await` and `gather`: groups of tasks, timeouts, cancellation and limits on how much runs at once.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

**Cancellation** arrives as `asyncio.CancelledError` at the task's current await. Clean up in `finally`, and never swallow it (for example with `except BaseException`), or the task cannot be stopped.

`async for` loops over async iterators (streamed rows, websocket messages), and `async with` enters async context managers (HTTP sessions, pooled connections). asyncio is single-threaded: it helps while waiting on the network or a disk, not while computing.

visual.title: One task fails inside a TaskGroup

messages.note: The block raises an ExceptionGroup: handle it with except*

visual.title: Async toolbox
rows: **Structured concurrency**: the block waits for every task, and one failure cancels the rest
Results in order, with failures returned as values
Failures go unnoticed unless awaited, and an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected
Cancel slow work and raise TimeoutError
At most 20 coroutines inside a section at once
A bounded job stream: producers wait when it is full (**backpressure**)
visual.caption: All live in `asyncio`: write `asyncio.TaskGroup()`, `async with asyncio.timeout(5):` and so on.

sections.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name, delay, fail=False):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # stands in for I/O
    if fail:
        raise ConnectionError(f"{name} failed")
    return f"{name}: ok"

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(fetch("slow", 1.0))
            tg.create_task(fetch("bad", 0.1, fail=True))
    except* ConnectionError as group:
        print("failed:", [str(e) for e in group.exceptions])

    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):
            await fetch("slow", 1.0)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("slow: timed out")

asyncio.run(main())
sections.tip: The in-browser playground runs ordinary scripts, not an event loop, so try this code in a local Python 3.11 or newer.
sections.pitfall: Calling a coroutine function without awaiting it. `fetch("users")` alone only creates a coroutine object; nothing runs, and Python warns that it was never awaited.

check.question: Inside async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg, one of three tasks raises ConnectionError. What happens?
choices: The other tasks are cancelled, and the block raises an ExceptionGroup containing the ConnectionError
The ConnectionError is raised at once while the other tasks keep running in the background
Nothing happens until you call result() on the failed task
The other tasks keep running and the error is only logged
check.explanation: TaskGroup is structured concurrency: a failure cancels the siblings, the block waits for them to finish, and the errors come out together in an ExceptionGroup.

keyTerms.definition: A function bundled with variables from the enclosing scope that it uses, kept alive after the outer function returns.
A callable that takes a function and returns a replacement, applied with @name above a def; @d def f is f = d(f).
A function that takes arguments and returns a decorator, as in @retry(times=3).
A decorator for wrapper functions that copies the wrapped function's name, docstring and other metadata.
The __enter__ and __exit__ methods a with statement calls for setup and guaranteed cleanup; a true return from __exit__ suppresses the exception.
A generator statement that yields every item of another iterable or generator, used for delegation and recursion.
A chain of generators where each stage pulls items lazily from the previous one, processing data in constant memory.
Caching a function's results by its arguments so repeated calls return the stored value; functools.cache and lru_cache provide it.
A type checker refining a value's type after a check such as is not None or isinstance.
A typing class describing required methods or attributes; any class that has them matches, without inheriting (structural typing).
A type hint describing a dict's keys and the type of each value, used for JSON-like data.
The match statement (Python 3.10+), which compares a value against sequence, mapping and class patterns and binds the parts.
Linking a new exception to the one that caused it, explicitly with raise New() from err (__cause__) or implicitly (__context__).
An exception (Python 3.11+) that carries several exceptions at once, handled with except*.
A tool such as cProfile that measures how often each function runs and how much time it takes, so you optimize the real bottleneck.
Running tasks inside a scope such as asyncio.TaskGroup that waits for all of them and cancels the rest if one fails.

summary: A decorator replaces a function with a wrapper: use functools.wraps, return the result, add a factory layer for arguments.
Context managers guarantee cleanup; with @contextmanager, put the yield inside try/finally.
Generators chain into lazy pipelines; itertools and functools replace many loops and caches.
Advanced hints pay off only when a checker such as mypy runs.
Translate low-level errors with raise ... from err and handle them once, where you can act.
Profile before optimizing, and keep async work bounded and cancellable.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate who knows basic Python what really happens when Python sees @retry(times=3) above a function, and why the wrapper needs functools.wraps and a return statement.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

a = make_counter()
b = make_counter()
a()
a()
print(a(), b())
questions.explanation: Each call to make_counter creates a new count variable, and each returned closure keeps its own. a has been called three times by the print, b once. nonlocal is what lets increment rebind count instead of creating a local.

questions.question: add(2, 3) prints "calling add" and then None. What is the bug?
choices: The decorator must be applied as @log() with parentheses
functools.wraps discards the wrapped function's return value
*args cannot carry two positional arguments
wrapper calls func but never returns its result, so it returns None
questions.explanation: The caller gets whatever wrapper returns. Without `return func(*args, **kwargs)`, wrapper falls off the end and returns None. wraps only copies metadata, and @log() would be needed only for a decorator factory.

questions.question: Complete the decorator factory so @repeat(times=3) works.
choices: func
decorator
repeat
wrapper
questions.explanation: repeat(times=3) is called first and must return the real decorator, which Python then applies to the function. Returning wrapper would skip a layer: Python would call wrapper(func) as if it were the decorator.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
choices: NameError: i is not defined
questions.explanation: Closures capture variables, not values. All three lambdas share the comprehension's i, which is 2 when they are finally called. Bind the current value with a default argument, lambda i=i: i, to get [0, 1, 2].

questions.question: A module contains @timed above def report(), and later calls report(). Put what happens in order.
items: The def statement creates the original report function
timed(report) runs and returns a wrapper
The name report is bound to the wrapper
report() is called, which runs the wrapper
The wrapper calls the original function and returns its result
questions.explanation: Decoration happens once, when the def executes. Every later call goes through the wrapper, which is why a print in the decorator body appears at import time, but a print in the wrapper appears on each call.

questions.question: In `with make_connection() as conn:`, what is conn bound to?
choices: None, unless the block raises
The object make_connection() returns, always
Whatever make_connection().__enter__() returns
The return value of __exit__
questions.explanation: as binds the result of __enter__. Files return themselves, so the two look the same there, but a manager can return something else entirely, like a cursor or a temporary path.

questions.question: After a with block that uses this manager raises an exception, the lock stays held forever. Why?
choices: contextmanager only works with files
The exception is raised at the yield, so release() never runs; wrap the yield in try/finally
yield must return the lock, or the with statement fails
acquire() must be called after the yield
questions.explanation: When the with block raises, contextmanager throws the exception into the generator at the yield. Code after the yield runs only on the success path unless it is in a finally block.

questions.question: What does this print?
choices: A, then B
Only A
A ZeroDivisionError traceback
Only B
questions.explanation: __exit__ returns True only for ZeroDivisionError, so 1 / 0 is swallowed and A prints. For the ValueError it returns False, so the error propagates and the outer except prints B.

questions.question: Which jobs are a natural fit for a context manager? Select all that apply.
choices: Opening a file and closing it
Holding a lock during a critical section
Beginning a transaction, then committing or rolling back
Changing a setting temporarily and restoring it
Converting a list to a set
Sorting a list in place
questions.explanation: Context managers pair a setup with a cleanup that must run even when the block fails. Converting or sorting has nothing to undo afterwards.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def gen():
    yield 1
    yield from [2, 3]
    yield 4

print(sum(gen()))
questions.explanation: yield from [2, 3] yields 2 and then 3, so the generator produces 1, 2, 3, 4, which sum to 10.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
limit = 2
gen = (x for x in range(5) if x < limit)
limit = 4
print(list(gen))
questions.explanation: The condition runs only when list() pulls items, and by then limit is 4. Only the first iterable, range(5), is evaluated when the generator expression is created.

questions.question: normalize() returns [] instead of [0.25, 0.5, 1.0]. Why?
questions.code:
def normalize(values):
    top = max(values)
    return [v / top for v in values]

readings = (int(s) for s in ["2", "4", "8"])
print(normalize(readings))
choices: max() consumed the generator, so the comprehension loops over nothing; pass a list
int() returns strings inside a generator expression
Division by top is integer division, which rounds to 0
max() cannot take a generator, so top is None
questions.explanation: max() pulled every value to find the largest, leaving the generator exhausted. The comprehension then gets no items and returns []. Passing list(...) or a list comprehension fixes it.

questions.question: Complete flatten so it handles lists nested to any depth.
choices: yield flatten(item)
return flatten(item)
flatten(item)
yield from flatten(item)
questions.explanation: yield from passes along every value the recursive call produces. yield flatten(item) would yield a generator object, return would stop the whole generator, and a bare call creates a generator that never runs.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
from itertools import accumulate
print(list(accumulate([2, 5, 1, 7], max)))
questions.explanation: accumulate with max keeps the largest value seen so far: 2, then max(2, 5) = 5, then max(5, 1) = 5, then max(5, 7) = 7.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
from itertools import groupby
words = ["apple", "bob", "avocado", "banana"]
print([k for k, _ in groupby(words, key=lambda w: w[0])])
choices: ['apple', 'bob', 'avocado', 'banana']
questions.explanation: The first letters are a, b, a, b, and groupby starts a new group every time the key changes. Sort the words by their first letter first to get ['a', 'b'].

questions.question: Match each itertools function with what it does.

pairs.right: Walks several iterables as if they were one
Takes a slice of any iterator, even an infinite one
Yields fixed-size chunks; the last may be shorter
Every combination across inputs, like nested loops
Running totals or another running result

questions.explanation: These six cover most of the loops people write by hand. All of them are lazy and return iterators.

questions.question: How many tuples does itertools.combinations(range(5), 2) produce?
questions.explanation: Choosing 2 of 5 items where order does not matter: 5! / (2! * 3!) = 10. permutations(range(5), 2) would give 20, because (0, 1) and (1, 0) both count.

questions.question: This raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. What is the fix?
choices: Add maxsize=None to the decorator
Use lru_cache instead, which accepts lists
Return a float instead of an int
Pass a tuple such as total((1, 2, 3)), because cache keys must be hashable
questions.explanation: cache and lru_cache both key a dict by the arguments, so neither accepts lists. Convert to a tuple at the call site, or cache a helper that takes a tuple.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
from functools import partial

def power(base, exp):
    return base ** exp

square = partial(power, exp=2)
print(square(7))
questions.explanation: partial fixed exp=2, so square(7) calls power(7, exp=2), which is 7 squared.

questions.question: Which function is a bad candidate for @cache?
choices: def slugify(title: str) -> str: ...
def parse_version(text: str) -> tuple[int, ...]: ...
def current_price(symbol: str) -> float: ...  # asks a live market API
def fib(n): ...
questions.explanation: A live price changes over time, so a cached answer goes stale and is returned forever. The other three always give the same output for the same input.

questions.question: What does functools.reduce(fn, items, initial) do, and why pass initial?
questions.answer: It folds the items into one value by calling fn(accumulator, item) for each item, starting from initial. Without initial, an empty input raises TypeError.
questions.explanation: reduce(operator.mul, nums, 1) multiplies everything together. When a built-in such as sum, max or math.prod exists, it is clearer than reduce.

questions.question: mypy reports an error on this function. What is it about?
questions.code:
def greet(name: str | None) -> str:
    return "Hi " + name.upper()
choices: String concatenation needs an f-string
name may be None, which has no upper method; check for None first
str | None is invalid syntax in a hint
The return type should be str | None
questions.explanation: mypy says: Item "None" of "str | None" has no attribute "upper". Add `if name is None: return "Hi"` before, and the checker narrows name to str for the rest of the function.

questions.question: Match each typing tool with what it expresses.

pairs.right: Any object with the required methods, no inheritance needed
A dict with specific keys and value types
A function that takes an int and returns a str
Links input and output types in a generic function

questions.explanation: These are the tools you will meet most often beyond basic hints, in library code and in FastAPI or Pydantic models.

questions.question: Which statements about Python type hints are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Python does not enforce them when the program runs
typing.cast converts the value to the new type at runtime
A function returning Any disables checking of how callers use its result
A Protocol lets a class satisfy an interface without inheriting from it
Adding hints makes CPython run the code faster
questions.explanation: Hints are for tools. cast only informs the checker and returns the value unchanged, and CPython ignores hints when executing, so they do not speed anything up.

questions.question: Complete the signature so a checker knows last([1, 2]) returns an int.
questions.code:
def last[T](items: list[T]) -> _____:
    return items[-1]
choices: T
Any
object
list[T]
questions.explanation: Returning T ties the result to the element type of the argument. Any would turn checking off, and object would force callers to narrow before using the int.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2

print(Color(2).name)
questions.explanation: Calling the enum class with a value looks up the member with that value, Color.GREEN, and .name is its name as a string.

questions.question: Python refuses to run this file: SyntaxError: name capture 'DONE' makes remaining patterns unreachable. Why?
questions.code:
DONE = "done"

def label(status):
    match status:
        case DONE:
            return "finished"
        case _:
            return "open"
choices: Constants must be defined inside the function
match cannot compare strings
A bare name in a case is a capture pattern that matches anything; use a literal or a dotted constant like Status.DONE
case _ must come first
questions.explanation: case DONE would assign the subject to a new local named DONE and always match, so case _ could never run. Python makes that a SyntaxError. Literals (case "done") and dotted names (case Status.DONE) compare by value.

questions.question: Task is declared with @dataclass(slots=True) and has a field named title. What does t.titel = "x" do?
choices: Raises AttributeError
Creates a new attribute titel
Silently changes title
Raises TypeError because dataclasses are frozen
questions.explanation: With slots there is no per-instance __dict__, so only the declared fields can be set. Without slots, the typo would quietly create a second attribute and title would keep its old value.

questions.question: Which case patterns match the dict {"type": "key", "key": "q", "shift": True}? Select all that apply.
choices: `case {"type": "key", "key": k}:`
`case {"type": "key"}:`
`case {"type": "key", "key": "q", "ctrl": True}:`
`case {"type": "click", **rest}:`
`case {"shift": True, **rest}:`
questions.explanation: Mapping patterns match when the listed keys exist with matching values; extra keys are ignored. The ctrl pattern needs a key the dict does not have, and the click pattern needs a different type.

questions.question: A traceback contains the line "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". What does it usually tell you?
choices: The code used raise ... from err correctly
The exception was retried automatically
Two threads raised exceptions at the same time
A new exception was raised inside an except block without from, often a bug in the handler
questions.explanation: Implicit chaining (__context__) shows when an exception occurs while another is being handled. A deliberate translation with from err prints "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" instead.

questions.question: Complete the line so the KeyError is kept as the explicit cause of UserNotFound.
choices: except err
from err
with err
as err
questions.explanation: raise NewError(...) from err sets __cause__ to err. from None would hide the KeyError instead.

questions.question: Where should an exception be handled and logged, and why not at every level?
questions.answer: At the layer that can act on it (retry, show a message, return an error response), usually the top of a request handler or main(). Logging at every level writes the same error many times and hides where it is really handled.
questions.explanation: Lower layers should let exceptions propagate, translating them at module boundaries if needed. One handler at the top logs once with logger.exception, traceback included.

questions.question: Which failures are reasonable to retry with backoff? Select all that apply.
choices: A timeout calling a payment API that accepts an idempotency key
HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
ValueError from parsing a malformed date
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, after the Retry-After delay
KeyError from a misspelled dict key
questions.explanation: Retry transient failures on operations that are safe to repeat. A parse error or a typo fails identically every time, so retrying only delays the real error.

questions.question: A loop checks `if order_id in seen:` 100,000 times, where seen is a list of 100,000 ids. What is the best fix?
choices: Run the loop in a thread pool
Sort the list first
Use a while loop instead of for
Build seen as a set, so each check is O(1) on average
questions.explanation: in on a list scans it, so the loop costs billions of comparisons. A set answers each check by hashing. Sorting alone does not help, because in does not use binary search.

questions.question: Which standard-library profiler do you run with python -m to list every function's call count and cumulative time?
questions.explanation: python -m cProfile -s cumulative app.py runs the script under the profiler and sorts the report by cumulative time. The pure-Python profile module gives the same report with more overhead, and timeit is for timing small snippets, not whole programs.

questions.question: Put the steps for speeding up slow code in order.
items: Make the code correct, with tests
Measure the slow case with realistic input
Profile to find the biggest cumulative cost
Fix the algorithm or data structure there
Re-measure, and keep the change only if it helps
questions.explanation: Tests first, so optimizing cannot silently break behavior. Measuring and profiling point at the real cost, and re-measuring proves the change was worth its complexity.

questions.question: fetch is defined with async def. What does the statement fetch("users") do on its own?
choices: Runs fetch in a background thread
Runs fetch to completion and discards the result
Creates a coroutine object without running the body
Raises SyntaxError outside an async function
questions.explanation: Calling a coroutine function only builds the coroutine. It runs when awaited or scheduled as a task; otherwise Python warns that it was never awaited.

questions.question: Complete the line so fetching the price gives up after 2 seconds with TimeoutError.
choices: sleep
timeout
gather
Semaphore
questions.explanation: asyncio.timeout(2) cancels the block's work after 2 seconds and raises TimeoutError. sleep would just wait, and Semaphore limits concurrency rather than time.

questions.question: You must fetch 5,000 URLs, and the API allows at most 20 requests in flight. Which approach fits?
choices: An asyncio.Semaphore(20) acquired around each request
A threading.Lock around each request
asyncio.gather on all 5,000 coroutines with no limit
time.sleep(0.05) between requests inside each coroutine
questions.explanation: The semaphore lets 20 requests run at once and makes the rest wait their turn. Unlimited gather can trip rate limits and exhaust sockets, time.sleep blocks the whole event loop, and a lock allows only one request at a time.

questions.question: This worker cannot be stopped with task.cancel(). Why?
choices: queue.get() cannot be cancelled
Cancellation only works on tasks created by TaskGroup
except BaseException catches asyncio.CancelledError and keeps looping, swallowing the cancellation
continue inside an async function is a SyntaxError
questions.explanation: cancel() raises CancelledError (a BaseException subclass) at the current await. Catching it and continuing ignores the request. Catch Exception for job errors, or re-raise CancelledError.
